title: Unique Paths
description: Brute force to optimized: recursive exploration of both moves versus a 2D bottom-up DP grid.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: A robot starts at the top-left corner of an m x n grid and wants to reach the bottom-right corner, moving only right or down at each step. Return the number of distinct possible paths.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","grid dimensions m, n"],["Output","Number of distinct paths from top-left to bottom-right"],["Goal","dp[i][j] = number of ways to reach cell (i,j), built from the cell above and the cell to the left"],["Constraints","Up to 100 by 100 grid"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Count paths on a grid, moving only right or down\"","A classic 2D DP: the number of ways to reach a cell equals the sum of ways to reach the cell above it and the cell to its left"]]}

blocks.text: Since the robot can only move right or down, reaching any cell (i, j) must come from EITHER the cell directly above (i-1, j) OR the cell directly to the left (i, j-1). So the number of distinct paths to (i, j) is simply the SUM of the paths to reach each of those two cells. Cells in the very first row or first column have exactly 1 path (a straight line from the start).

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Routes Through a City Grid Moving Only East or South
blocks.text: Picture counting the number of distinct routes through a city grid, where you can only travel east or south at each intersection. The number of routes to reach any intersection is exactly the sum of the routes reaching the intersection just north of it and the one just west of it.

blocks.caption: Ways to reach a cell = ways to reach the cell above + ways to reach the cell to the left

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every cell in the first row can only be reached by moving right repeatedly from the start, so it has exactly 1 path; similarly for the first column (moving down repeatedly).

Observation 2: For any other cell, since the robot can only arrive from above or from the left, the number of paths to it is the SUM of the paths to those two neighboring cells.

Observation 3: Filling this grid row by row (or column by column) from the top-left, the bottom-right cell ends up holding the total answer.
This leads to a 2D bottom-up DP grid, with the first row and column initialized to 1, and every other cell summing its top and left neighbors.
Recursively try both possible moves (right, down) from every cell, without memoization, counting how many recursive paths reach the destination.
Why the code is written this way

items: Trying both moves recursively directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same cells repeatedly across many different paths, costing exponential time; a 2D DP grid computes each cell exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(2 raised to (m+n)) without memoization.
Space: O(m+n) recursion depth.
Limitation: a 2D DP grid computes each cell's path count exactly once, reusing the top and left neighbors directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build an m by n grid dp, with every cell in the first row and first column set to 1. For every other cell (i, j), set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]. Return dp[m-1][n-1].
Use a 2D bottom-up DP grid, filling the first row and column with 1, and summing the top and left neighbors for every other cell.
Dry run for m=3, n=2 (a 3 row by 2 column grid)

Since the robot can only move right or down, every cell's path count is fully determined by exactly its top and left neighbors' already-computed path counts, and the first row and column have a trivially known count of 1 (a single straight-line path); building the grid in row-major order ensures both needed neighbors are always already computed by the time each cell is processed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times n).
Space: O(m times n), reducible to O(n) using a single rolling row.

blocks.text: Unique Paths is the foundational 2D grid DP problem: every cell's answer combines exactly its top and left neighbors.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "a cell's path count is the sum of its top and left neighbors" is the core insight, directly connecting this to Pascal's triangle-style combinatorics.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "count paths on a grid moving only right or down", think: 2D DP summing the top and left neighbors.

items: How would you solve this with a direct combinatorial formula instead, using binomial coefficients (choosing which moves are "down" among all moves)?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(2^(m+n)); the 2D DP grid costs O(m times n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: 2D bottom-up dynamic programming on a grid.
Core Idea: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], since a cell can only be reached from above or from the left.
Time: O(2^(m+n)) for the brute force, O(m times n) for the DP approach.
Space: O(m+n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(m times n) (reducible to O(n)) for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: the first row and column always have exactly 1 path each.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, easy to medium 2D DP problem.
One line memory trick: sum of the cell above and the cell to the left.
